strengths: Clear and relevant contribution: dynamic, ASR-guided frame merging addresses an important bottleneck for speech language models and provides a single codec operating across unusually low average frame rates.
Strong low-rate results: at 6.25 Hz, FlexiCodec substantially improves RVQ-1 intelligibility over retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines while maintaining competitive reconstruction metrics.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering semantic and acoustic reconstruction, bitrate-matched public codecs, ASR probing, TTS, audio understanding, and phoneme-level analysis.
Ablations provide concrete support for the main design choices, including dynamic versus fixed-rate encoding, ASR versus SSL features, FSQ, and the merging/unmerging Transformers.
The dynamic-rate mechanism is simple and interpretable; its correlation with phoneme density and the visualized alignments provide useful evidence that allocation responds to linguistic complexity.

The paper is clearly organized and supplies substantial architecture, optimization, baseline-retraining, and parameter-count details. The proposed downstream TTS system also demonstrates meaningful autoregressive speedups.
weaknesses: The thresholds used to obtain the headline 8.3 Hz and 6.25 Hz operating points were selected through trials on the test set, introducing test-set contamination. Thresholds should be calibrated on a validation set and then frozen.

The claimed controllability is imprecise: a threshold controls only the dataset-dependent average rate, not an exact per-utterance bitrate, and downstream TTS supports only three discrete control settings rather than the claimed continuous 3–12.5 Hz range.

Comparisons are confounded by FlexiCodec's frozen 234M-parameter ASR encoder trained on 300k hours, giving a total system size of 450M and a large external-data advantage over many baselines. Encoding latency, memory, and total computational cost are not reported despite efficiency claims.

Evaluation is concentrated on clean English read speech, largely within the LibriSpeech/LibriLight domain. Robustness to noisy, conversational, accented, multilingual, music, and out-of-domain audio is not established.
The method is non-streaming and uses bidirectional Transformers. This limits practical codec applications and weakens claims concerning edge devices or adaptive transmission.

The strongest TTS quality uses a conventional 50 Hz NAR acoustic representation, so the end-to-end system does not fully realize low-frame-rate generation. The subjective study is also small—only ten utterances per system—with no significance testing, and the reported confidence intervals overlap substantially.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: the paper calls acoustic quality state of the art despite mixed metric wins, and suggests broader real-world benefits without evaluating real-world data.

Reproducibility remains partly prospective: the anonymous manuscript contains blank demo/model links, and the promised code release cannot be verified from the paper itself. Some evaluation details, such as statistical uncertainty for codec metrics and exact computational comparison protocols, are missing.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/83468cecd57040e19162f7ca5b664b24/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: reducing speech-token sequence length while retaining intelligibility, with potential benefits for autoregressive speech models.

FlexiCodec combines ASR-guided token merging, dual semantic/acoustic streams, and rate control in a coherent architecture. Its 6.25 Hz RVQ-1 reconstruction WER is substantially better than the retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines.

The paper includes useful component studies: fixed-rate comparisons, merging/unmerging Transformer ablations, alternative semantic features, FSQ versus VQ, ASR probing, and a correlation analysis relating token and phoneme rates.

The downstream TTS study suggests that low-rate semantic tokens can reduce autoregressive inference time while retaining reasonable intelligibility, and the paper provides many implementation and training details.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has direct test-set leakage: the thresholds used to obtain 12.5, 8.3, and 6.25 Hz are explicitly selected through trial runs on the LibriSpeech test set that is subsequently used for reporting results. Thresholds should be selected on a validation set and then frozen; this problem undermines the central rate-matched comparisons.

The claimed continuously controllable 3–12.5 Hz operating range is overstated. Only a few threshold settings are evaluated, the threshold-to-rate mapping is corpus dependent and does not guarantee a requested rate for an individual utterance, and performance at 3 Hz is poor (51.5% RVQ-1 WER and 18.1% RVQ1:8 WER). The TTS system supports only three discrete control settings.

Evidence for general-purpose audio compression is narrow: codec training and primary testing are confined to English audiobook speech, principally LibriLight/LibriSpeech test-clean. There is no evaluation on noisy speech, conversational speech, multilingual or code-switched data, music, or general audio, despite broader codec and audio-understanding claims.

The acoustic-quality claims rely almost entirely on automatic proxies such as narrowband PESQ, UTMOS, MCD, and speaker similarity. No human listening test is reported for codec reconstructions, and UTMOS even rates some reconstructions above the ground truth, illustrating the limitations of these proxies.

Efficiency is characterized mainly through output frame rate and downstream TTS RTF. The paper does not report codec encoding/decoding latency, FLOPs, memory, or real-time performance, even though inference uses a 234M-parameter frozen ASR encoder in addition to 216M trainable codec parameters and requires full-utterance processing. This weakens the low-latency and edge-device motivation.

Baseline evidence is uneven. The strongest low-rate comparisons rely on author-retrained variants whose hyperparameter tuning and training parity are insufficiently documented, while the larger open-source comparison mixes checkpoints trained on different data and objectives. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests for codec metrics or ablations labeled as significant.

The TTS comparison is confounded by differing architectures and decoding setups, and its best-quality configuration still uses a 50 Hz NAR acoustic representation. The subjective evaluation is small—six experts rating only ten samples per system—and reports dispersion rather than confidence intervals or significance tests, so several claimed quality differences are not well supported.

Much of the gain appears attributable to directly quantizing features from a large supervised ASR model; the novelty beyond combining this strong semantic prior with adjacent-frame thresholding and averaging is moderate given prior variable-rate tokenization and dual-stream codecs. The audio-understanding results are likewise partly expected from inheriting SenseVoice representations and do not isolate the contribution of dynamic tokenization.

The paper does not discuss consent, impersonation, or misuse risks associated with its zero-shot TTS experiments, despite presenting voice imitation capability as a downstream application. Overall, the promising clean-speech results do not compensate for test-set tuning, limited external validation, incomplete efficiency accounting, and claims broader than the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for speech language models: reducing codec sequence length while retaining semantic content. Supporting dynamic average rates below 10 Hz and inference-time rate control is practically meaningful.

FlexiCodec combines ASR-guided merging, dual semantic/acoustic streams, FSQ semantic quantization, and local-attention merging/unmerging modules into a coherent end-to-end system. The method is clearly described and technically plausible.

The core results are strong. At 6.25 Hz, FlexiCodec obtains 4.15% RVQ-1 reconstruction WER versus 31.5% for the strongest retrained baseline, while also achieving favorable acoustic metrics. Comparisons include both carefully retrained low-rate baselines and numerous publicly available codecs across bitrate regimes.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering reconstruction intelligibility and quality, probing, phoneme-rate correlation, component ablations, audio understanding, and downstream TTS. The fixed-rate ablations provide concrete evidence that dynamic allocation improves semantic preservation, particularly at 6.25 Hz.

The TTS results demonstrate practical downstream value: low-rate AR generation substantially improves inference speed while remaining competitive with established systems in intelligibility, speaker similarity, and reported perceptual quality.

The paper provides substantial implementation detail, including architectures, losses, optimization settings, bitrate accounting, baseline modifications, and parameter breakdowns, and states that code and models will be released.
weaknesses: The thresholds for the principal 12.5, 8.3, and 6.25 Hz evaluations were selected using trial runs on the test set. This is test-set leakage; thresholds should be calibrated on a validation set and then frozen before evaluation.

The novelty is partly incremental: the central merging rule is adjacent-frame cosine-threshold segmentation followed by averaging, while the architecture draws heavily on existing dual-stream codecs, token merging, ASR features, FSQ, and local-attention Transformers. Much of the large gain appears attributable to using a strong supervised ASR representation rather than dynamic-rate modeling itself; the dynamic-rate ablation improves RVQ-1 WER from 5.22% to 4.15% at 6.25 Hz but has little effect on PESQ or UTMOS.

The claim of useful controllability down to 3 Hz is overstated. At 3 Hz, RVQ-1 WER rises to 51.5% and RVQ-1:8 WER to 18.1%, so this operating point provides controllability but not convincing semantic preservation. Moreover, downstream TTS only evaluates three predefined rate settings rather than continuous control.

Evaluation is concentrated on clean English read speech, despite broader framing as an audio codec. There is no multilingual, code-switched, noisy, conversational, music, long-form, or streaming evaluation, and the authors acknowledge the multilingual and streaming limitations.

The subjective TTS study is small: six experts evaluate only ten samples per system. Sampling and assignment details, blinding, inter-rater agreement, significance tests, and whether the displayed uncertainty is a standard deviation or confidence interval are not provided, limiting the strength of perceptual-quality claims.

Efficiency reporting focuses on downstream token-generation speed but does not adequately characterize codec encoding/decoding cost, latency, memory, or real-time performance. This matters because inference uses a frozen 234M-parameter ASR encoder and a 216M-parameter trainable codec; the reported 216M parameter count understates the full 450M system footprint.

Several reproducibility and presentation issues remain: the manuscript contains blank demo/model-release links, the claimed supplementary code cannot be assessed from the paper itself, the mapping from threshold to realized rate is data-dependent, and some baseline comparisons mix retrained and official systems with heterogeneous training data and architectures. These do not invalidate the results but prevent a stronger acceptance score.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck for speech language models: reducing codec frame rate while retaining semantic content and reconstructability.
The content-adaptive merging mechanism is simple, interpretable, inference-time controllable, and supported by a strong correlation between allocated frame rate and phoneme density.
Results at 6.25–12.5 Hz are compelling, especially RVQ-1 semantic preservation; at 6.25 Hz, the reported WER of 4.15% substantially improves over the retrained DualCodec baseline's 31.5%.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering reconstruction, ASR probing, TTS, audio understanding, efficiency, out-of-domain speech, multilingual transfer, and multiple acoustic and semantic metrics.

Ablations are informative: fixed-rate retraining directly supports the benefit of dynamic allocation, while the extended and factorial analyses clarify that ASR features provide the largest gain and dynamic rate provides a further consistent improvement.
The paper is generally clear, technically detailed, and provides substantial training and architecture information.
weaknesses: The frame-rate thresholds are selected using trial runs on the test set, creating test-set leakage. Threshold-to-rate calibration should be performed on a held-out validation set, followed by untouched test evaluation.

The claim of useful controllability down to 3 Hz is overstated: at 3 Hz, RVQ-1 WER is 51.5% and RVQ1:8 WER is 18.1%. The evidence supports a broad rate-quality tradeoff, but not strong semantic preservation throughout the claimed 3–12.5 Hz range.

Codec quality is assessed almost entirely with objective proxies. No listening study directly compares codec reconstructions with strong baselines, despite high-fidelity audio reconstruction being a central claim; UTMOS and PESQ alone are insufficient for this conclusion.

Baseline comparisons are imperfectly controlled. FlexiCodec has 216M trainable parameters plus a 234M frozen ASR encoder, while several key baselines are much smaller, and bitrate categories remain broad rather than strictly matched. Training compute, capacity, and pretraining advantages are not isolated.

The main improvement is driven primarily by substituting ASR features for SSL features, while the proposed dynamic mechanism gives a smaller incremental WER gain. This makes the novelty of the overall performance advance less decisive than the headline comparisons suggest.

The TTS subjective evaluation is small—six evaluators rating only ten samples per system—and lacks significance testing and sufficient detail about sample assignment. Some baseline numbers are borrowed from official reports, limiting strict comparability.
Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted PDF: the advertised code and demo links are blank, results lack variance across runs, and several evaluation/calibration details are underspecified.

The method is non-streaming, relies on a large frozen ASR model, and its semantic tokens generalize poorly zero-shot to several non-English languages. The limitations section also incorrectly says multilingual evaluation was not conducted despite extensive multilingual results in the appendix.
Potential misuse of the demonstrated zero-shot TTS capability, such as voice impersonation, is not discussed or mitigated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reducing speech-token sequence length below 10 Hz while retaining intelligibility and reconstruction quality. A single codec supporting variable rates is practically appealing.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering reconstruction, semantic probing, TTS, audio understanding, out-of-domain speech, multilingual transfer, efficiency, and several component ablations.

The controlled fixed-rate ablation provides evidence that dynamic allocation helps semantic preservation: at 6.25 Hz, RVQ-1 WER improves from 5.22% to 4.15%, with smaller gains for RVQ1:8 and acoustic metrics.

Results on clean English speech are strong. In particular, FlexiCodec substantially improves RVQ-1 WER over the retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines at 6.25 Hz, while offering competitive objective reconstruction metrics.
The manuscript is generally understandable and provides substantial architectural, optimization, bitrate-accounting, and parameter-breakdown details.
weaknesses: The main performance gain is not attributable to the proposed dynamic-rate mechanism. The factorial analysis shows that replacing w2v-BERT-2 with SenseVoice reduces RVQ-1 WER from 31.5% to 5.99%, whereas dynamic allocation supplies a much smaller improvement. Thus, much of the headline advantage comes from a powerful 234M-parameter ASR encoder pretrained on 300k hours rather than the central dynamic-codec contribution.

Comparisons do not adequately control for this external supervision and computation. Table 5 reports only 216M trainable parameters for FlexiCodec while omitting its frozen ASR encoder from that column; the complete model has 450M parameters. Baselines use different pretrained representations, datasets, architectures, and parameter budgets, making the state-of-the-art claims difficult to interpret.

The merging rule itself is a simple greedy thresholding of adjacent ASR-feature cosine similarities. Given closely related dynamic-token-merging and low-rate-codec work, the methodological novelty is moderate, and the paper does not compare directly against dynamic-rate codec baselines such as CodecSlime, TFC, or VARSTok under a common setup.

Several evaluation choices use test data for configuration: frame-rate thresholds are selected through trials on LibriSpeech test-clean, and language-specific thresholds are similarly determined on the evaluated multilingual data. This creates avoidable test-set leakage and weakens the reported comparisons.

Claims of high-quality reconstruction rely almost entirely on imperfect objective predictors. UTMOS even rates some reconstructions above ground truth. No human listening evaluation is reported for the codec itself, and the referenced audio demonstrations are unavailable in the submitted manuscript.

The TTS subjective study is too small and underspecified: only six raters and ten utterances per system are reported, without a clear assignment design, confidence-interval procedure, randomization protocol, or significance testing. The TTS baselines also differ in training data and architecture, limiting causal claims about the codec frame rate.

Evidence that token allocation follows phonetic information density is suggestive but incomplete. The utterance-level correlation can be confounded by speaking rate and silence, while the boundary analysis contains only four qualitative examples sharing the same transcript. Boundary precision/recall against phoneme or syllable boundaries would be more convincing.

The claimed controllable 3–12.5 Hz range is overstated: thorough codec evaluation focuses on 6.25, 8.3, and 12.5 Hz, while performance deteriorates sharply at 3 Hz to 51.5% RVQ-1 WER. Downstream TTS is likewise tested at only three operating points.

Scope and generalization remain limited. The model is non-streaming, trained primarily on English read speech, and its semantic stream catastrophically fails zero-shot on several non-English languages. These limitations matter for the broad framing as a general neural audio codec.

Reproducibility is incomplete because the code and demo links are blank, despite the manuscript stating that these resources are available. The substantial compute requirements and dependence on a specific pretrained ASR model further raise the replication barrier.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for speech language models: reducing codec sequence length while retaining semantic content and reconstructible acoustics. Controllable dynamic rates below 10 Hz are practically meaningful.

FlexiCodec combines ASR-guided semantic features, adaptive frame merging, dual-stream quantization, and frame unmerging in a coherent architecture. The inference-time rate control from a single trained model is a useful capability.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it includes retrained low-rate baselines, bitrate-matched comparisons, component ablations, ASR probing, TTS, audio understanding, efficiency measurements, and out-of-domain and multilingual tests.

Results at 6.25 Hz are compelling, particularly the RVQ-1 reconstruction WER of 4.15% versus 31.5% for the strongest retrained baseline. The downstream TTS results also demonstrate a concrete efficiency benefit without a large quality loss.

The factorial analysis usefully distinguishes the contributions of ASR features, dynamic allocation, Transformer refinement, and FSQ. It candidly shows that ASR features provide the largest gain while dynamic rates add a smaller but consistent improvement.
The method and training setup are described in substantial detail, including architectures, losses, optimization, bitrate accounting, parameter breakdowns, and baseline modifications.
weaknesses: The central novelty is less decisive than the headline results suggest. Most of the semantic improvement comes from replacing SSL features with features from a very large ASR model pretrained on 300k hours; at 6.25 Hz, this change reduces WER from 31.5% to 5.99%, whereas dynamic allocation improves the comparable fixed-rate result from 5.22% to 4.15%. The paper should more carefully separate representation-pretraining gains from the proposed dynamic-rate mechanism.

The evidence that merging locally allocates tokens according to phonetic complexity is limited. The reported correlation is only at the utterance level, where speech rate naturally correlates with both phoneme rate and the number of dissimilar adjacent ASR frames. Local boundary metrics, comparisons against simple silence/speech-rate heuristics, and stronger allocation baselines would better substantiate the mechanism claim.

The merging thresholds for the headline 12.5, 8.3, and 6.25 Hz conditions were selected using trial runs on the test set. Even if this merely targets average rate, validation-set calibration would avoid test-set leakage and produce a cleaner comparison.

Despite audio reconstruction quality being a central claim, codec evaluation relies entirely on objective or learned metrics. A sufficiently powered human listening study of codec reconstructions is missing. The TTS listening study is small—six raters evaluating ten samples per system—and lacks significance tests and detailed protocol information.

Comparisons with recent variable-rate codecs are primarily qualitative because TFC, VARSTok, and CodecSlime are not included experimentally. An adapted dynamic-rate baseline or a simple ASR-guided selection baseline would clarify whether the proposed merging and refinement machinery is necessary.

The claim of useful controllability down to 3 Hz is overstated: at approximately 3 Hz, RVQ-1 and RVQ-1:8 WER deteriorate to 51.5% and 18.1%, respectively. The paper demonstrates technical rate control across this range, but not consistently usable quality.

Some reproducibility and accounting details are inconsistent or unclear, including parameter counts across the main description, speed table, and parameter breakdown. The blank code/demo links in the reviewed manuscript also prevent verification of the claimed resource release.

The codec depends on a large, non-streaming ASR encoder and performs poorly for unseen-language RVQ-1 representations. These limitations narrow deployment applicability, while potential voice-cloning, privacy, and misuse risks of the TTS capability are not discussed.
